WorkDetail:
This project proposes three areas of exterior building improvements that are within the public space. Those three areas are the northeast building corner, southeast building corner, and along the 7th street building frontage. The purpose of this project is to provide a new café seating area and enhance the pedestrian ingress/egress experience for the building. The total land disturbance for this project will be less than 5,000 square-feet. 

Firstly, the northeast public space improvements consist of one 8-feet marquee building projection and the replacement of the existing stairs and handrail with new granite stairs and handrail. 

Secondly, the southeast public space improvements consist of one 8-feet marquee building project, one 5-ft marquee building projection, one new café seating area, stairs, and handrails. Additionally, due to the existing topography adjacent to the café seating area, there is a 36-inch maximum height retaining wall and handrail. 

Lastly, the public space improvements along 7th Street SE consist of expanding the existing grass strip, new brick pavers sidewalk, two new gas firepits, overhead string lights, granite pavers at the building entrance, one 8-feet marquee building projection, and a new turf area.

WorkDetail:
The General Services Administration (GSA) and USSS are
upgrading Officer Posts at President’s Park (PRPA) to meet current
USSS operational requirements.   Existing posts do not meet current
USSS requirements. Upgrades follow recommendations from the
PRPA 2022 Master Plan and Security Assessment and are currently
being implemented in a series of projects across the campus.
The project includes a prioritized grouping of posts at GSA
managed property at the New Executive Office Building (NEOB)
and the Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB). The EEOB
and NEOB posts are located in the west and northwest of PRPA,
typically along 17th Street and H Street; two are located within the
NEOB garage. These officer posts facilitate pedestrian and vehicular
access to President’s Park at the EEOB and NEOB. For context, all
Posts under this project are shown on the site map, but highlighted
Posts A and C at the NEOB are the only Posts that impact the public
space and required for further definition in this presentation.
An Officer Post is inclusive of the booth, barriers and all security
measures constructed at the location.
The project will improve posts to meet current USSS operational
requirements and security standards. Upgrades to vehicular
access control and security elements associated with several posts
are also included in this project. Updates to post elevations and
exterior materiality would align with the architectural precedents by
established posts across the park, while respecting the construction
and styles used at the adjacent buildings. The project does not
change the site’s use or staff capacity.

WorkDetail:
Installation and commissioning of two Digital Entrance Displays at the north and south entrances of the Dupont Circle Metrorail Station, located at 1525 20th Street NW and 1351 19th Street NW, respectively. The work area at each location is approximately 5 ft × 5 ft.
The scope includes all labor, materials, equipment, and integration with existing electrical and communication systems necessary to deliver fully operational displays. The system will comply with WMATA standards and all applicable codes.
All design work will be performed in-house by WMATA’s structural, electrical, and architectural engineering teams. Installation activities related to electrical and communication systems will also be carried out internally by WMATA’s Electrical Low Voltage and Communications teams, ensuring consistency with agency standards, streamlined coordination, and quality control throughout the project lifecycle.
The display unit specifications are as follows: 55-inch screen, 1920 × 1080 resolution, power input of 115–230 VAC, overall dimensions of 842 × 1870 × 174.5 mm, and an approximate weight of 188 kg per sign.
DOB and DDOT have agreed with WMATA to apply for a permit for the Dupont Circle north and south station screens under a new TOPS category created specifically for WMATA display screens. The permit will require that no advertising be displayed and that a maintenance agreement be established.
WMATA is currently working to obtain final approval from the Public Space Committee, as well as a letter of support from the ANC and a maintenance agreement between WMATA and DDOT.
Once completed, the maintenance agreement, ANC support letter, and site plan drawings will be forwarded to DDOT, either in person or by mail.
TypeDetailNames: Fixture; WMATA Transit Digital Display
NeighborhoodNames: Dupont Circle, Connecticut Avenue/K Street

WorkDetail: Work previously approved under #392820. Mixed-use first floor retail and residential above with 82 residential units and one level of subgrade parking. Please note that sheet C-102 shows that an existing street closure was processed for Burnham Place between Parkside Place and Kenilworth Terrace NE in 2009 and is currently private property. The existing curb cut alignments in public space are being modified to decrease in width. Burnham Place will be one-way circulation from south to north. Private Burnham Place will also hold loading activities as well as garage entry. This project proposes all DDOT standard streetscape elements. No non-standard elements are proposed in public space. As discussed in the PDRM held on 3/8/2022, public space along Parkside Place NE is not wide enough to accommodate both the minimum tree box width of 4 ft and the minimum ADA width of 6 ft. The project proposes the minimum street tree box width of 4 ft and the remaining width to building face (including less than 1 ft into private property) will maintain clear sidewalk width for pedestrians. Parkside Place curb cut proposes a replacement of the existing eastern ADA ramp and a proposed receiving ADA ramp and crosswalk for pedestrians given surrounding intersection and as-built conditions. Kenilworth Terrace proposes a receiving ADA ramp for approved and issued permit #358092.

WorkDetail:
POLE RESTORATION: Trinidad Avenue NE and Public Alley
•	We will excavate a hole as wide as diameter of the pole and about 8 inches away from the pole.
•	We then hand dig down to a depth of 36 – 60 inches.
•	Using Non-Conductive soil probes, probing in areas where soil cannot be unearthed.
•	A steel truss is then placed in the hole, against the pole.
•	Using a fiberglass support pole, a pneumatic jack hammer is raised to a height of about 8 Ft.
•	Using the jack hammer, the truss is driven into the ground at total depth of 5 to 5.5 feet deep depending on pole size.
•	The truss is then banded to the pole in two locations. The first location 15 to 26 inches above groundline and at 50-55 inches above groundline at the top of the truss.
•	The removed dirt will be replaced. The surrounding work area will be cleaned of other debris and unused installation material
•	A cap will then be placed over the top of the truss.
•	The truss is then painted with a cold galvanizing compound paint to prevent corrosion.

WorkDetail:
This application proposes to activate the public space at the 2nd Street Underpass (commonly known as BridgeSpot), located beneath the I-695 Southeast Freeway at 2nd Street SE. This activation follows DDOT's infrastructure improvements to the underpass and seeks to establish a permanent, multi-use public amenity space serving residents of Capitol Hill, Navy Yard, Southwest, and surrounding communities.
Proposed Improvements and Amenities:
Multi-Sport Court (Basketball & Futsal): Installation of a regulation-sized multi-use sport court with painted markings for both basketball and futsal, including standard basketball backboards and goals, futsal goal markings, and appropriate surfacing to support safe athletic use.
Skatepark: Construction of a skatepark facility consisting of permanent concrete or prefabricated skate elements including ramps, rails, ledges, and transition features, designed to accommodate beginner and intermediate skill levels for youth and adult skaters.
General Community Public Space: Development of open, flexible public space for passive and active community use, including seating, wayfinding/signage, and any additional safety elements not addressed by DDOT's rehabilitation, to facilitate safe pedestrian movement through the underpass as a neighborhood cut-through.
Purpose and Public Benefit:
The activation of BridgeSpot addresses a documented need to transform the underpass into a welcoming, safe, and vibrant community destination. The I-695 freeway has historically functioned as a physical barrier between neighborhoods; this project supports DDOT's and the District's goals of reconnecting communities, activating underutilized public infrastructure, and improving pedestrian safety and comfort. All amenities are intended for free, unrestricted public use.
Community Engagement:
The Capitol Riverfront BID has already undertaken meaningful community engagement to ensure BridgeSpot reflects the needs of the people who will use it most. To date, the BID has hosted public activation events at the underpass and facilitated design workshops with residents, youth, skateboarders, and stakeholders from Capitol Hill, Navy Yard, Southwest, and surrounding neighborhoods. The feedback gathered has directly shaped the proposed amenity mix, and the BID is committed to continuing this community-centered process through design, permitting, and construction.

WorkDetail:
Installation and commissioning of two Digital Entrance Displays at the north and south entrances of the Dupont Circle Metrorail Station, located at 1525 20th Street NW and 1351 19th Street NW, respectively. The work area at each location is approximately 5 ft × 5 ft.
The scope includes all labor, materials, equipment, and integration with existing electrical and communication systems necessary to deliver fully operational displays. The system will comply with WMATA standards and all applicable codes.
All design work will be performed in-house by WMATA’s structural, electrical, and architectural engineering teams. Installation activities related to electrical and communication systems will also be carried out internally by WMATA’s Electrical Low Voltage and Communications teams, ensuring consistency with agency standards, streamlined coordination, and quality control throughout the project lifecycle.
The display unit specifications are as follows: 55-inch screen, 1920 × 1080 resolution, power input of 115–230 VAC, overall dimensions of 842 × 1870 × 174.5 mm, and an approximate weight of 188 kg per sign.
DOB and DDOT have agreed with WMATA to apply for a permit for the Dupont Circle north and south station screens under a new TOPS category created specifically for WMATA display screens. The permit will require that no advertising be displayed and that a maintenance agreement be established.
WMATA is currently working to obtain final approval from the Public Space Committee, as well as a letter of support from the ANC and a maintenance agreement between WMATA and DDOT.
Once completed, the maintenance agreement, ANC support letter, and site plan drawings will be forwarded to DDOT, either in person or by mail.
TypeDetailNames: Fixture; WMATA Transit Digital Display
NeighborhoodNames: Dupont Circle, Connecticut Avenue/K Street

WorkDetail: This site plan proposed the construction of a two-story senior wellness center on the existing grounds of Kramer Middle School. Forty-five parking spaces, including two ADA compliant and one van accessible parking space, are proposed for use of the wellness center. The parking designated for the school is proposed to be restriped to allocate forty-five parking spaces, including two ADA compliant and one van accessible parking space. New utility connections are proposed for connection to the senior wellness center including a 6" sanitary sewer connection, a 2.5" domestic water connection, and a 3" fire connection. Stormwater management controls will be provided on-site via bioretention planters, bioswales, and an increase in pervious area. These controls will connect via gravity pipe systems and outfall into a storm sewer which traverses through the site.

WorkDetail:
POLE RESTORATION: 
•	We will excavate a hole as wide as diameter of the pole and about 8 inches away from the pole.
•	We then hand dig down to a depth of 36 – 60 inches.
•	Using Non-Conductive soil probes, probing in areas where soil cannot be unearthed.
•	A steel truss is then placed in the hole, against the pole.
•	Using a fiberglass support pole, a pneumatic jack hammer is raised to a height of about 8 Ft.
•	Using the jack hammer, the truss is driven into the ground at total depth of 5 to 5.5 feet deep depending on pole size.
•	The truss is then banded to the pole in two locations. The first location 15 to 26 inches above groundline and at 50-55 inches above groundline at the top of the truss.
•	The removed dirt will be replaced. The surrounding work area will be cleaned of other debris and unused installation material
•	A cap will then be placed over the top of the truss.
•	The truss is then painted with a cold galvanizing compound paint to prevent corrosion.

NeighborhoodNames: Mayfair, Hillbrook, Mahaning Heights

WorkDetail:
POLE RESTORATION: 
•	We will excavate a hole as wide as diameter of the pole and about 8 inches away from the pole.
•	We then hand dig down to a depth of 36 – 60 inches.
•	Using Non-Conductive soil probes, probing in areas where soil cannot be unearthed.
•	A steel truss is then placed in the hole, against the pole.
•	Using a fiberglass support pole, a pneumatic jack hammer is raised to a height of about 8 Ft.
•	Using the jack hammer, the truss is driven into the ground at total depth of 5 to 5.5 feet deep depending on pole size.
•	The truss is then banded to the pole in two locations. The first location 15 to 26 inches above groundline and at 50-55 inches above groundline at the top of the truss.
•	The removed dirt will be replaced. The surrounding work area will be cleaned of other debris and unused installation material
•	A cap will then be placed over the top of the truss.
•	The truss is then painted with a cold galvanizing compound paint to prevent corrosion.

WorkDetail:
POLE RESTORATION: 
•	We will excavate a hole as wide as diameter of the pole and about 8 inches away from the pole.
•	We then hand dig down to a depth of 36 – 60 inches.
•	Using Non-Conductive soil probes, probing in areas where soil cannot be unearthed.
•	A steel truss is then placed in the hole, against the pole.
•	Using a fiberglass support pole, a pneumatic jack hammer is raised to a height of about 8 Ft.
•	Using the jack hammer, the truss is driven into the ground at total depth of 5 to 5.5 feet deep depending on pole size.
•	The truss is then banded to the pole in two locations. The first location 15 to 26 inches above groundline and at 50-55 inches above groundline at the top of the truss.
•	The removed dirt will be replaced. The surrounding work area will be cleaned of other debris and unused installation material
•	A cap will then be placed over the top of the truss.
•	The truss is then painted with a cold galvanizing compound paint to prevent corrosion.

WorkDetail:
On behalf of the Central Community Development Corporation (CCDC), I am writing to request a written determination regarding whether a permit is required to install two temporary public art banners on the exterior of our building located at:

Congress Heights Arts & Culture Center (CHACC)
3200 Martin Luther King Jr. Avenue SE
Washington, DC 20032

The proposed installation is part of CCDC's application to the District of Columbia Commission on the Arts and Humanities FY27 Public Art Building Communities Grant. The project will transform the exterior of the Congress Heights Arts & Culture Center into a highly visible public art display by installing two large-scale temporary banners featuring original artwork that celebrates the culture, history, and identity of the surrounding community. The installation is intended to increase public access to art while contributing to the visual character of the neighborhood.

The proposed banner dimensions are:

Banner 1: 140" × 75"
Banner 2: 300" × 70"
The banners are proposed to be installed for the period of October 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027, after which they will be removed.

The banners will be securely attached to the existing accessible rooftop balcony/railing of our building and allowed to hang down the exterior façade. No ground disturbance, excavation, structural alterations, or scaffolding will be necessary for the installation or removal of the banners.

For your reference, I have attached images of the building identifying the proposed banner locations and dimensions. I have also included a sample artwork image to illustrate the type and style of public art we intend to showcase. The sample image is provided for conceptual purposes only and does not represent the final artwork.

We respectfully request a letter indicating whether this proposed temporary banner installation requires a permit under your department's regulations. If a permit is not required, we would greatly appreciate written confirmation stating that determination. If additional reviews, approvals, or permits are necessary, please let us know the appropriate process or direct us to the appropriate office.

This letter will support our FY27 Public Art Building Communities Grant application and help ensure our project proceeds in compliance with all applicable District regulations.

WorkDetail:
The project will repair and replace existing fence that borders the public sidewalk in front of the house (516 1st St, SE).  The existing fence is constructed of 4 brick columns, one at each end of its length and two at the center from which an iron gate is hung.  Iron railing is mounted in two segments to the brick columns.  Below the iron railings there is a low, brick knee wall that rises only 6 inches above grade.  (See attached photos of Fence Project Existing Conditions.)  The mortar in the brick columns and knee wall has deteriorated, so the fence is failing.  The project will replace with similar structures both the two brick columns located at the property borders and the knee wall.  The two brick columns near the center of the fence line, to which the gate is attached, will be replaced with architecturally salvaged cast iron fence posts approximately 5 inches in diameter.  The posts are appropriate to the age of the house, which was built in 1890, and they are similar to posts on the front stairs that are original to the house.  The existing iron railings and iron gate will be replaced with ironwork similarly appropriate to the house and also obtained through architectural salvage.

The two segments of the existing fence are approximately of equal length, with the gate between the segments.  The footings for the brick column on the south segment have been disturbed by the intrusion of tree roots and will need to be replaced.  There is no surface evidence that the footings on the north segment are not entirely sound, but they will be inspected when the existing columns and knee wall are removed, and they will be repaired or replaced as necessary.  All new footings will be 30 inches deep and extend 2 inches on each side of the brick columns.  The maximum amount of land that will be disturbed to repair and/or install new footings will be 6 square feet, including the footings for the cast iron posts that will replace the existing two center columns.  

The footings for the cast iron posts (which at their base – their widest point – are only 5.5 inches square) will not need to be as large as those for the existing brick columns (which are 12 inches square).  Their footings will extend a minimum of 2 inches on each side of the post bases but may be extended 4 inches on each side for additional stability.  

The proposed project site has been visited by Matt Lehtonen, the Lead Urban Forrester in DDOT’s Urban Forestry Division.  He recommended that possible damage to the roots of a Special Tree that is near the construction area be minimized by limiting the footprint of the footings as much as possible.  He will be contacted and his recommendations followed for any roots of 2 inches or more in diameter that may be encountered when digging the footings.

WorkDetail:
This application seeks to activate the 200-block of Virginia Avenue SE, in SMD 6B01, as a publicly accessible basketball/futsal facility. A note on the block designation:the permit area corresponds to what mapping systems display as 138–198 Virginia Avenue SE. Those addresses do not exist in DDOT's TOPS address database; the application therefore uses the 200-block range that TOPS recognizes for this segment.
The permit area lies south of Garfield Park (Res 17, Sq 736-S, A&T L 800) within and adjacent to the Virginia Ave SE right-of-way, a variable-width public street, beginning at the intersection of Virginia Ave SE, 2nd St SE, and H St SE and terminating where the bicycle/ADA ramp from Garfield Park meets the Virginia Ave SE sidewalk. The permit area comprises approx 23k sf of DDOT right-of-way, of which the proposed court enclosure occupies 82'-0" × 58'-0" (4,756 square feet). In addition to the court and its related infrastructure (which includes permanent basketball hoops, moveable futsal goals, modular sports walls and netting, artistic elements and sponsorship elements - per language passed in the most recent Budget Support Act), the application includes secured electrical outlet bollards, as well as planters and an operable gate system to prevent unauthorized auto access to protect all users of the space (DDOT has already installed signage barring unauthorized vehicles, which has gone unheaded). The basketball court, deployment of electrical fixtures, and securing of the road were all discussed with DDOT's Garfield Park Connector team and incorporated into the final designs. Details for all project elements including product specifications are included in the application.
The permit area is a dead-end spur terminating at the New Jersey Ave SE overpass at the before the U.S. Capitol Power Plant grounds, where the remainder of the Virginia Ave SE block through
to S. Capitol St has been fenced off. Given the unique federal jurisdiction and security demands of the area and the absence of traffic demand, the roadway is not expected to be
reintegrated into the transportation network. The segment carries no through movements, serves no curb cuts or loading, and provides access to no occupied property, making it a rare candidate for public-space conversion as long as all access to overpass infrastructure is maintained - which the applicant commits to.
The permit area lies beneath the I-695 structure within the recorded easement for bridge purposes (L. 11594 F. 129). The lowest vertical clearance beneath the structure in the area of the proposed
improvements is 18'-2", providing > 8' of clearance above the 10'-0" upper containment netting and > 4' above bball goal. The easement is controlled by DDOT, and no coordination with any other party is required.
The Applicant previously established a pickleball facility within the same block under a public space permit application that DDOT has approved and that is pending issuance. That facility now attracts daily users and demonstrates the demand for recreational programming in this right-of-way. This application builds on it by converting a further portion of the DDOT right-of-way into a basketball and futsal court. The proposed amenities complement Garfield Park's existing tennis courts, children's playgrounds, and open green space.

WorkDetail:
1399 New York Ave NW has a Pepco vault with a solid slab lid at the sidewalk level. This requires the vault to be mechanically cooled with two large air conditioners. Along with the cost of electricity, air conditioners require regular preventive maintenance to keep them running efficiently to prevent the Pepco equipment from overheating since the vault lid is solid concreate that prevents the heat from naturally rising out of the vault. We have been trying to schedule maintenance of the HVAC system for the past two years and finally got traction with Pepco who notified us that we must completely shut down power to the building twice a year to perform the maintenance. As you can probably imagine, this a both extremely disruptive and costly for the building (about $11k per occurrence). The equipment is at the end of its useful life and we would like to switch the vault lids over to the grates that are all around the city. Pepco has given us the okay to proceed but they advised that we get DDOT’s approval first.
We believe that switching to the grates will save money in the long run for the building and also save energy which furthers the District’s push toward energy efficiency.

WorkDetail:
The following is a list of stormwater reduction practices or technologies that are permitted to be installed on public space as part of the 
Program: A. Rain Barrels as defined as a large container, generally five feet (5’) in height, used to capture and store the rainwater running 
through a downspout from the roof. Rain Barrel installations taller than seven feet (7’) shall not be installed on public space. The overflow 
from rain barrels installed on public space and authorized by this MOU should lead to the same collection point as did the original 
downspout. Rain Barrels shall not be installed on public space at the front of properties in historic districts unless there is sufficient space for 
screening and/or to be contained within the landscape. B. Rain Gardens as defined as a small garden landscaped to collect, store and 
infiltrate stormwater runoff in its loose amended soil and strategically placed to intercept stormwater runoff until it can be fully absorbed 
into the ground. Rain gardens authorized by this MOU shall not contain underdrains that connect to sewer lines in public space. C. Pervious 
pavement as defined as any paved surface that permits water to soak naturally into the ground to replace existing impervious surfaces. At 
properties where no public sidewalks exist, existing lead walks and driveways may be replaced with pervious pavement between the 
property line and the curb line of the roadway subject to the terms of the RiverSmart Homes Maintenance Agreement (“Maintenance 
Agreement”) as provided below. D. Shade Trees as defined as a large tree with a widespread, dense canopy. A selection of shade trees native 
to the Chesapeake Bay region has been chosen by DDOE that will benefit homeowners as well as the local watersheds. E. Bayscaping as 
defined by vegetation that is native to the Chesapeake Bay region to replace existing lawn area. Template Bayscaping gardens have been 
developed by DDOE that will benefit homeowners and reduce pollution to local watersheds.

The Park Road construction site is located at Park Road NW (2000–2199 block, east side) at the townhome driveway and NPS trail, just south of Piney Branch Parkway NW. Construction work includes: constructing the Park Road shafts, ventilation vault and associated structures; relocating the sanitary sewer; installing electrical equipment, light poles and handholes; and restoring the site to its original condition after project completion.

The scope of work within the DDOT right-of-way (approx. 7,107 SF, per drawing C-53) includes: tree removal; establishing the construction entrance, staging area boundaries and traffic maintenance devices; installing electrical conduit, handholes and cabinet for temporary and permanent power; installing light poles; sewer relocation/improvement, including installation of two (2) manholes (PR-SMH-01 and PR-SMH-02) and adjustment of existing structures to final grade; and site restoration after project completion (curb and gutter, sidewalk, roadway, driveway and trees).

Staging and maintenance of traffic will be covered under a separate DDOT public space occupancy permit.

WorkDetail:
POLE RESTORATION: 
        In the Public Alley Rear of 1629 Fort Dupont Street SE we will excavate a hole as wide as diameter of the pole and about 8 inches away from the pole. 
        We then hand dig down to a depth of 36-60 inches.
·	Using Non-Conductive soil probes, probing in areas where soil cannot be unearthed.
·	A steel truss is then placed in the hole, against the pole.
·	Using a fiberglass support pole, a pneumatic jack hammer is raised to a height of about 8 FT.
·	Using the jack hammer, the truss is driven into the ground at total depth of 5 to 5.5 FT deep depending on pole size.
·	The truss is then banded to the pole in two locations. The first location 15-26 inches above groundline and at 50-55 inches above groundline 
         at the top of the truss.
·	The removed dirt will be replaced. The surrounding work area will be cleaned of other debris and unused installation material
·	A cap will then be placed over the top of the truss.
·	The truss is then painted with a cold galvanizing compound paint to prevent corrosion.
TypeDetailNames: Over Head Work; Pole Installation (single or first one)
NeighborhoodNames: Twining, Fairlawn, Randle Highlands, Penn Branch,

WorkDetail:
POLE RESTORATION:  
        In the Sidewalk of South Capital Street SE we will excavate a hole as wide as diameter of the pole and about 8 inches 
        away from the pole. We then hand dig down to a depth of 36-60 inches.
·	Using Non-Conductive soil probes, probing in areas where soil cannot be unearthed.
·	A steel truss is then placed in the hole, against the pole.
·	Using a fiberglass support pole, a pneumatic jack hammer is raised to a height of about 8 FT.
·	Using the jack hammer, the truss is driven into the ground at total depth of 5 to 5.5 FT deep depending on pole size.
·	The truss is then banded to the pole in two locations. The first location 15-26 inches above groundline and at 50-55 inches above 
         groundline at the top of the truss.
·	The removed dirt will be replaced. The surrounding work area will be cleaned of other debris and unused installation material
·	A cap will then be placed over the top of the truss.
·	The truss is then painted with a cold galvanizing compound paint to prevent corrosion.

WorkDetail:
LOCATION: Public 
         Alley Rear 1145 46th Place SE Pole Restoration: We will excavate a hole as wide as diameter of the pole and about 8 inches away from the pole.
         We then hand dig down to a depth of 36-60 inches.
·	Using Non-Conductive soil probes, probing in areas where soil cannot be unearthed.
·	A steel truss is then placed in the hole, against the pole.
·	Using a fiberglass support pole, a pneumatic jack hammer is raised to a height of about 8 FT.
·	Using the jack hammer, the truss is driven into the ground at total depth of 5 to 5.5 FT deep depending on pole size.
·	The truss is then banded to the pole in two locations. The first location 15-26 inches above groundline and at 50-55 inches above 
        groundline at the top of the truss.
·	The removed dirt will be replaced. The surrounding work area will be cleaned of other debris and unused installation material
·	A cap will then be placed over the top of the truss.
·	The truss is then painted with a cold galvanizing compound paint to prevent corrosion.

WorkDetail: One (1) proposed boring on the exterior of 1445 New York Ave NW performed from the public sidewalk adjacent to New York Ave NW. Work is not anticipated to block sidewalk access. The geotechnical boring will be approx. 4 inches in diameter and is necessary to obtain geotechnical information for designing the foundations of the proposed renovations at 1445 New York Ave NW. The boring will be started by coring through the sidewalk surface and further advanced utilizing wash-rotary drilling methods to an approx. depth of 70 ft below grade.
